parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a hostile federal layer with a strongly protective division. Universal federal exposures dominate: passport/visa marker restrictions (Supreme-Court-upheld, X markers halted, travellers stranded), a visa cable directing refusal where sex is in doubt with possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, exclusion from federally funded single-sex facilities, and documented federal custody abuse of trans detainees (beatings, solitary, sexual abuse). One state's bathroom arrest (men's ward for 24 hours) shows custodial misplacement risk. Against this, the division offers full gender-identity civil-rights coverage, hate-crime enhancement, no facility ban, easy marker changes, protected care, a pro-access high-court ruling, and a 'low-risk' 2026 assessment — but these cannot offset federal entry, custody, and facility rules the dossier shows operating.

entry_documents.exposure: Feb 2025 halt on X/mismatched markers; Nov 2025 Supreme Court let restrictions take effect; travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, stranded abroad; Feb 2025 visa cable directs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, with lifetime fraud-ineligibility consideration; 8+ foreign governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports valid to expiry; fraud finding requires four elements, limited waivers, never automatic; civil-liberties suit pending in national courts; legal-aid FAQ exists.
entry_documents.interaction: Division licence/birth-certificate marker changes do not travel: the visitor's home passport governs entry and every federal document check, so friendly state document practice is bypassed at the border.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) from 2026; immigration custody reports of forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse against trans men; reporting on trans prisoners ceased 2025. Division correctional facility houses a trans woman by gender identity.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division prison placement follows gender identity (documented, resident-sphere); habeas and courts formally available nationally; several federal orders enjoined.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor's document discrepancy can escalate from border questioning into federal custody, where the hostile federal custody regime — not the division's protective placement practice — applies.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Executive order bars trans people from federally funded single-sex facilities nationwide; 22+ state/province facility bans mapped (9 all government buildings etc.), 4 states criminalise in circumstances; a trans student was arrested and held 24h in a men's ward under one such trespass law (Mar 2025).
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has no facility-restriction law and its high court ruled (2014) for identity-congruent bathroom access; 29 states plus capital district lack bans.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal funding and executive-order reach can pull division spaces (federally funded buildings) under the national rule despite state law; visitor using a federal building in the division is exposed.

care_services.exposure: Oct 2025 proposed federal rule barring insurance reimbursement for under-18 trans care; subpoenas of under-19 patient records (summer 2025); EO framing care as 'mutilation'; division university system complied with federal sports restrictions after funding threat.
care_services.protection: Division: care explicitly protected (Apr 2024 law), 16-17-year-olds may access hormones since Jul 2023, conversion therapy on minors banned since 2019, SOGI data mandate from Oct 2026.
care_services.interaction: Division protections hold for state-level care, but federal funding levers, DOJ subpoenas and insurance rules can reach providers and records even here; whether sports compliance persists is uncertain.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal orders criminalise teachers facilitating social transition, label care 'mutilation', direct law-enforcement investigation of 'gender ideology'; Dec 2025 reward memo and May 2026 counterterrorism strategy referencing 'radically pro-transgender' groups; 66% public support for binary document rules; genocide-stage comparisons by advocates.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Reward criteria do not list gender ideology as a trigger; strategy states counterterrorism powers won't target mere disagreement; division retains pro-equality political culture (protections survived 2005 veto; 2021 law written in).
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal threat-framing sets the climate a visitor enters at airports and federal sites; division tolerance cushions street-level encounters but not official encounters.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal orders target minors' care and teachers aiding social transition; proposed insurance ban for under-18 care; hospital-record subpoenas; 27 states ban youth care; sports compliance in division's university system; sanctuary bill for trans minors shelved Jan 2024.
minors_guardians.protection: Division protects youth care (2023/2024 laws), bans conversion therapy on minors, allows minor marker changes with parental consent; national hate-crime statute covers bias violence.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling family's minor accessing division-authorized care may still encounter federal insurance, funding and investigative reach; guardian could face state inquiry via the criminal-prosecution directive elsewhere.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Documented bathroom arrest with men's-ward holding (Mar 2025, first under that state's law) signals police enforcement of facility rules in some units; national bias-crime statistics show persistent bias incidents; 4 states criminalise facility use; no division-specific violence figures.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; division hate-crime penalty enhancement and abolished trans-panic defence (2019); division public-accommodations protections since 2005; risk assessment groups division as low-risk (Jul 2026).
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Division police operate under protective state law, but encounters can escalate to federal framing; the arrest case shows custodial misplacement (men's ward) follows even a misdemeanour stop.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Core federal measures (passport rules, EOs, proposed health rules) remain in litigation or partially enjoined, so exposure is real but shifting; no division enforcement statistics or trans-violence rates documented; 22 states lack gender-identity anti-bias law nationally.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Working division remedies: civil-rights enforcement since 2005, hate-crime enhancements, high-court pro-access precedent, legal-aid FAQ nationally, pending civil-liberties suit on passports.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A visitor's practical remedy depends on forum: division agencies will likely act, federal agencies follow the challenged orders; travellers may not be present long enough for litigation to resolve.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.15-A features routine arrest on document mismatch, months of pretrial custody with guard beatings, coerced confessions and non-functioning appeals. Here there is no documented routine arrest of visitors, division courts and civil-rights enforcement function, and hate-crime remedies exist. Federal custody abuse is contingent, not the default path. Materially safer.

0.35-B: unwritten stops, passport/phone confiscation, hours-long interviews, occasional fines, mostly released uncharged. Our dossier's visa-refusal-with-lifetime-ineligibility threat, stranded travellers and federal custody abuse are comparably severe and state-authored; division protections and functioning courts push slightly above it, so roughly equal-to-somewhat-higher.

0.75-C has trained respectful border staff, a tribunal hearing detention appeals, written reasons and compensation, with only brief detention. Ours lacks trained, restrained entry practice — instead an operative cable directs refusal on sex doubt and marker rules strand travellers. Federal facility bans and documented custody abuse sit well below this level.

0.45-D: mandatory registration, nightly hotel transmission, database flagging, but criminal charges rare and no lethal threat. Comparable structure — universal document exposure with administrative rather than custodial default — though our federal custody-abuse record and visa-fraud ineligibility threat are harsher, while our division protections are stronger; net similar.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets one system: a documented hostile federal layer plus a protective division, interacting at every stage. Entry is governed by federal passport/visa rules — markers fixed at birth, X halted, discretionary refusal and lifetime-fraud exposure — which the division's easy marker changes cannot touch. Everyday local life is comparatively safe: no division facility ban, binding pro-access precedent, full civil-rights coverage, hate-crime enhancement, protected care, and a 2026 low-risk grouping. But federal facilities, funding, custody and investigative reach override local tolerance where they intersect (arrest → men's ward precedent; document discrepancy → federal custody with documented abuse). Compounding punitive provisions and unresolved litigation keep the operative regime well below reduced-risk: protections cushion but do not cancel the universal federal exposures.
